transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Louise Schiavone.
Around 81 million people are expected to travel over Thanksgiving week.
But in California, where high tides and heavy rains are forecast, one mayor is urging residents
to change their plans, NPR's Eva Berger reports.
As Americans set their minds on pumpkin pie and cranberry sauce.
The weather is not cooperating.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Laurie said next week the city is expecting extreme high tides
and rain.
I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential starting
Monday afternoon and going into Wednesday afternoon.
Two atmospheric rivers, which are long bands of water vapor that dump rain on certain areas,
will hover over northern California and the Pacific Northwest.
On the Eastern Seaboard, a storm is forecasted to move through the Carolinas into New England.
Meteorologists say that storm won't be as bad as the one in California, but during a
busy travel week, any challenging weather can cause delays.
Eva Berger, NPR News.
The agrochemical company Bayer has agreed to pay billions of dollars to people who sued
the company alleging the weed killer Roundup caused their cancer.
A judge in Missouri approved the settlement Friday.
NPR's Will Stone has details.
Bayer could pay as much as $7.25 billion in the coming years.
That money will go to people who already have non-Hodgkin lymphoma or get diagnosed in the
future.
In a statement, the CEO of Bayer called the settlement a decisive milestone that will
mitigate pending and future litigation.
The World Health Organization's cancer agency has found that glyphosate, the main ingredient
in the company's weed killer Roundup, is probably carcinogenic to humans.
Prominent scientists in the field of environmental health have echoed those concerns, but the
company denies this is the case, and the Environmental Protection Agency has also said it does not
pose a risk to human health, though the agency is currently reevaluating that finding.
Will Stone, NPR News.
President Trump is threatening to hit U.S. tech companies with what he calls a tremendous
tax.
NPR's Greg Myrie reports the president is taking a different approach when it comes
to selling American technology overseas.
Trump says he wants the U.S. to keep the lead in AI, and he also said he won't allow U.S.
companies to build AI data centers outside the U.S.
However, Trump is the one allowing Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.
Nvidia's Jensen Wong lobbied Trump last year and persuaded the president to allow these
sales.
At PR's Greg Myrie, President Trump advises the tech companies if they build artificial
intelligence data centers in other countries, they'll be heavily taxed.
He said that Americans should welcome data centers in their neighborhoods.
The midterm elections ushered in a new class of Democrats on Capitol Hill promising to
heavily regulate the data center business.
This is NPR News in Washington.
A postmortem examination of the globally beloved Cincinnati Zoo hippo Fiona found that the
hat that Fiona swallowed two weeks ago was caught in the middle of her small intestine.
New leaders say it was too far into her digestive system for any type of care to help her.
Scientists have discovered a tiny area in the brain that appears to act as a link between
hearing and speaking.
John Hamilton has more on research in the journal science.
It's called Wernicke's area, and for more than a century it's been known as a place
where the brain processes incoming words.
But Dr. Eddie Chang of the University of California San Francisco says a study of 28 people found
Wernicke's area has another role.
In addition to the listening function, it also has a function for planning the words
that we're about to say next.
Just before a person speaks, a small group of neurons in Wernicke's area begin sending
signals that help organize the impending string of syllables.
The discovery of neurons involved in both input and output could help explain how children
learn to say the words they hear.
For NPR News, I'm John Hamilton.
The lockout is still expected in Major League Baseball next month after players rejected
management's proposal for an international amateur draft.
Players want larger signing bonus pools and more rewards for small market teams.
MLB's five-year collective bargaining agreement expires midnight December 1st.
Management is expected to immediately lockout players in the sport's 10th work stoppage
since 1972.
I'm Louise Quivone, NPR News, Washington.

topics.text: Around 81 million expected to travel for Thanksgiving; San Francisco mayor urges residents to avoid travel amid storms
Bayer agrees to pay up to $7.25 billion to settle Roundup cancer lawsuits, approved by Missouri judge
Trump threatens heavy taxes on U.S. tech companies building AI data centers overseas
Cincinnati Zoo's hippo Fiona necropsy finds swallowed hat lodged deep in small intestine
Scientists find brain area Wernicke's region also helps plan words before speaking, study in Science
Major League Baseball lockout expected next month after players reject international draft proposal
